data.title: Insider Buying: Wagners Holding Non-Executive Chairman Bought AU$401k Of Shares
data.description:
Investors who take an interest in Wagners Holding Company Limited (ASX:WGN) should definitely note that the Non-Executive Chairman, Denis Wagner, recently paid AU$4.51 per share to buy AU$401k worth of the stock. Although the purchase is not a big one, by either a percentage standpoint or absolute value, it can be seen as a good sign.

Trump has pledged to "unleash" American oil and gas and these 15 US stocks have developments that are poised to benefit.

The Last 12 Months Of Insider Transactions At Wagners Holding

In the last twelve months, the biggest single sale by an insider was when the insider, Joseph Wagner, sold AU$66m worth of shares at a price of AU$4.40 per share. That means that an insider was selling shares at slightly below the current price (AU$4.57). When an insider sells below the current price, it suggests that they considered that lower price to be fair. That makes us wonder what they think of the (higher) recent valuation. However, while insider selling is sometimes discouraging, it's only a weak signal. We note that the biggest single sale was 68% of Joseph Wagner's holding.

Over the last year we saw more insider selling of Wagners Holding shares, than buying. You can see the insider transactions (by companies and individuals) over the last year depicted in the chart below. By clicking on the graph below, you can see the precise details of each insider transaction!

Check out our latest analysis for Wagners Holding

For those who like to find hidden gems this free list of small cap companies with recent insider purchasing, could be just the ticket.

Does Wagners Holding Boast High Insider Ownership?

Looking at the total insider shareholdings in a company can help to inform your view of whether they are well aligned with common shareholders. A high insider ownership often makes company leadership more mindful of shareholder interests. It's great to see that Wagners Holding insiders own 31% of the company, worth about AU$279m. I like to see this level of insider ownership, because it increases the chances that management are thinking about the best interests of shareholders.

So What Do The Wagners Holding Insider Transactions Indicate?

The recent insider purchase is heartening. But we can't say the same for the transactions over the last 12 months. The recent buying by an insider , along with high insider ownership, suggest that Wagners Holding insiders are fairly aligned, and optimistic. data.title: Missed Mastercard's Run? Here Is What Holders Saw
data.description:

Investors who held Mastercard over the past year are up 21.9%, including dividends. That is a striking outcome next to those risks. If you were weighing an investment on 25 November 2025, what exactly in the public record might have justified taking that ride?

The Two Mastercard Stories Investors Had In Front Of Them

The shares cost US$546 at the start of the period, so anyone looking at Mastercard then had to decide which story felt more realistic.

The bullish Narrative saw Fair Value at US$642, 17% above the start price. It leaned on sustained revenue growth from global digital payment trends and partnerships with digital-first players like PayPal, Uber and Mercado Libre.

The more cautious Narrative put Fair Value at US$500, 9% below the start price. It assumed revenue growth of 3.1% a year and a future P/E of 38.3x over a 5 year window, with competition from stablecoins and digital wallets treated as a key risk.

What The Mastercard Evidence Actually Tested

Mastercard’s Q3 2026 figures, with revenue at US$9.8b and net income at US$4.6b against US$8.6b and US$3.9b a year earlier, plus a margin shift from 45.7% to 47.2%, leaned toward the optimistic case that assumed resilient economics and pricing. The US$38b swipe fee settlement process and ongoing UK and US scrutiny pulled the other way. Overall, the period cut both ways.

The hinge assumption was whether strong digital payments growth could coexist with rising regulatory and stablecoin pressure. For a different stock, you would test that by tracking revenue, profit and margin trends alongside any fee caps, settlement terms, or crypto-payment launches that might reshape economics.

What Mastercard's Recent Run Already Prices In

Today Mastercard trades at US$660 after a 21.9% gain over the past year, and the current cautious Narrative sees Fair Value below that price. Esteban, a Simply Wall St Community investor who wrote the Narrative, frames Mastercard as more than a card network.

The argument leans on a payments infrastructure that throws off high margins without heavy reinvestment. A buyer at today’s price has to believe Mastercard can keep growing its value-added services share of revenue faster than the core network without eroding returns.

"Mastercard is a toll-booth on global commerce that has quietly become something more interesting: a toll-booth that also sells the security cameras, the traffic data and the insurance. The company earns a fee on every transaction routed across its network without extending credit, holding inventory, or reinvesting meaningfully to grow. Capital expenditure was $489 million in FY2025 against $17.6 billion of operating cash flow, a capex intensity of 2.8%."

One Narrative disagrees with today's price. → See where this Narrative says Mastercard should trade

Looking One Step Beyond Mastercard

Mastercard highlights global spending habits. You could also watch who handles the spending promise itself.

Card networks move payments. Another business often carries the loan, the customer relationship, and the fraud filters behind each swipe.

It earns money by combining the payment rail with lending, rewards, and compliance systems built around individual users.

Where Mastercard mainly processes transactions, this other player lives deeper in credit risk and regulation.

If trust or rulebook pressure shifts, the ripple can look very different there.

data.title: Is Core Lithium (ASX:CXO) Above Fair Value After Its Restart?
data.description:
Core Lithium has restarted production and the stock has swung between long term losses and shorter term gains, which puts fresh attention on what investors are really paying for in relation to its sales. With the share price around A$0.24, the key issue is how that tag lines up with the revenue generated and expected from the restarted operations.

  • The share price is down about 56.0% over 5 years. This makes the current valuation question heavily about what the business can deliver on the top line from here.
  • The restart of the Finniss Lithium Operation and first spodumene concentrate shipment, supported by a A$290 million funding package, can influence how quickly sales, margins and cash flows build against that capital base.
  • The analysts covering Core Lithium have run their own numbers. See what analysts think Core Lithium's shares could be worth.

The stock's next move may depend on whether Core Lithium's current market value is well supported by its existing and prospective sales base.

Has Core Lithium Run Too Far on Sales?

P/S fits Core Lithium because the market is focused on what its sales stream from Finniss can support rather than on near term earnings. At around 43.5x P/S, the stock trades at a large premium to the Metals and Mining sector average of 74.9x but also above the 25.3x peer group level, which already reflects revenue based expectations for other producers. Despite the first spodumene cargo and long term Glencore marketing agreement, this price tag still embeds a rich sales multiple relative to many comparable miners.

The fair multiple that aligns more closely with Core Lithium's own mix of growth prospects, margins and risk sits well below the current P/S level. The model is heavily penalising the recent free cash outflows and project risk rather than offering a precise target. That gap signals that on this framework the stock screens as overvalued on revenue, so any investment case needs to lean on factors outside the current sales base to feel comfortable with the valuation. data.title: BlackBerry (TSX:BB) Rebounds Into Focus, Is The Stock Still Cheap?
data.description:
BlackBerry (TSX:BB) moved back into focus after an 8.38% daily gain that tracked a broader technology rebound, which followed Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO during a renewed AI trade.

Recent trading tells a mixed story for BlackBerry. The share price is CA$12.07 after a strong year to date, with a 131.23% year to date share price return, but a 30 day share price return that declined 6.36% as investors weigh upcoming earnings and QNX growth updates. Over a longer horizon, total shareholder return of 110.65% over one year and 135.74% over three years points to momentum that has been building rather than fading.

Scan how BlackBerry’s move fits into the wider rebound by comparing it with hand-picked tech and AI-linked stocks in the 4 AI small caps.

BlackBerry now trades only slightly below the average analyst target and at a deeper discount to some intrinsic value estimates. After that sharp move, does the current price still understate what this business could be worth?

Most Popular Narrative: 4% Undervalued

On the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St, BlackBerry’s fair value sits at CA$12.55, a touch above the last close at CA$12.07. This frames the recent rally as still slightly short of that central estimate.

The main thing that has to go right is that QNX converts its record royalty backlog, Alloy Kore design wins and growing embedded and physical AI pipeline into sustained high-margin revenue, while Secure Communications maintains its ARR base despite geopolitical risks.

The narrative that BlackBerry is fairly valued and bullish implies the current share price already reflects expectations for continued profitable growth, rising cash generation and the monetization of the company’s more than $1.2b QNX royalty backlog over time.

See why 16 investors see BlackBerry as 4% undervalued.

Result: Fair Value of CA$12.55 (UNDERVALUED)

Still, if QNX’s record royalty backlog underdelivers or Secure Communications’ US$221m ARR weakens, the current BlackBerry narrative could quickly look optimistic.

Find out about the key risks to this BlackBerry narrative.

Another View: BlackBerry Looks Expensive On Earnings

That 4% undervalued fair value story leans on cash flows and analyst targets. A straight P/E check tells you something different. BlackBerry trades around 62x earnings, while the North American software group sits near 30.7x and the fair ratio sits at 36.7x. That gap points to real valuation risk if sentiment cools.

Peers on average trade near 52x earnings, so even relative to similar companies the stock looks richly priced. The question for anyone running the numbers is simple. Does BlackBerry’s current profit profile really support this kind of premium, or is the market paying up for optimism?
